---
title: dangling references in coroutine
---

Given an `Object` class, which allows implicit conversion from classes like `String`.

```cpp
class Object
{
	Object(String s);
};
```

Implicit construction is allowed by design, since a `String` is also a valid `Object`. We don't want to write stuff like `Object(String("foo"));`{.language-cpp} to create a string object.

However, this can cause trouble is the following example.

```cpp
Task CreateTask(const Object& object);

Task<void> OK()
{
	Object object;
	Task task = CreateTask(object);
	co_await task(); // OK, object lives in the coroutine frame
}

Task<void> Error()
{
	String s;
	Task task = CreateTask(s); // creates a temporary object
	co_await task(); // FATAL ERROR: the temporary object is destroyed
}
```

`CreateTask()` creates a coroutine, which can be `co_await`ed. The const reference to `Object` is stored in the coroutine frame. The trap here is if we pass a `String`, which will be implicitly converted to a temporary `Object`, then the task will hold a dangling reference to the temporary `Object`. The temporary object is valid inside the `CreateTask()` function call and is destroyed once the function returns.

To keep benefits of implicit conversion and avoid the above trap:

```cpp
Task CreateTask(Object&&) = delete;
```

In C++, xvalues belong to rvalue category. By marking the the rvalue version of CreateTask as delete, the compiler will not create a temporary instance of `Object.`
